content: 1. Development of SMS-Based Tools for Malaria Monitoring in Uganda An innovative, cost-effective, and open-source tool utilizing short message service (SMS) technology was developed to monitor malaria in remote areas of Uganda. This tool was designed to improve accessibility and efficiency in tracking malaria cases in underserved regions. 2. SMS for Life: Improving Antimalarial Drug Supply in Tanzania A pilot project named SMS for Life was implemented in rural Tanzania to enhance the management of antimalarial drug supplies. This initiative utilized standard mobile phone technology to address stock-outs and ensure the availability of essential medications in remote healthcare facilities. 3. Mobile Phones for Drug and Medical Supply Access in Africa Mobile phone technology has been shown to improve access to drugs and medical supplies across Africa. This approach leverages the widespread availability of mobile devices to streamline logistics and enhance healthcare delivery in resource-limited settings. 4. Mobile Data Collection for Drug Logistics in Zambia Mobile phones were employed to collect end-line evaluation data for a pilot project on the essential drug logistics system in Zambia. This method demonstrated the potential of mobile technology in improving data collection and management for healthcare systems. 5. Preventing Stock-Outs of Antimalarial Drugs in Sub-Saharan Africa The World Health Organization (WHO) highlighted the success of Novartis' SMS for Life program in preventing stock-outs of antimalarial drugs in sub-Saharan Africa. This initiative utilized mobile technology to monitor drug availability and ensure timely replenishment. 6. Mobile Devices for Birth and Death Notifications The WHO is developing guidelines to inform investments in digital health approaches that use mobile devices for birth and death notifications. Ministries of health, donors, and decision-makers are increasingly recognizing the value of mobile technology in acquiring accurate and timely statistics on vital events. 7. Primary Objectives of Mobile-Based Birth and Death Notifications To evaluate the effects of birth notifications via mobile devices compared to standard practices. To assess the effects of death notifications via mobile devices compared to standard practices. 8. Secondary Objectives To describe the strategies used to implement mobile-based birth and death notifications. To identify factors influencing the implementation of these notifications. 9. Search Methods for Evidence Comprehensive searches were conducted in databases such as Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and others. Studies published after 2000 in any language were included. Citation searches and calls for papers were also issued to identify relevant studies. 10. Selection Criteria for Studies For primary objectives: Randomized trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series designs were included. For secondary objectives: Any study design (quantitative, qualitative, or descriptive) that explored strategies or factors influencing implementation was considered. 11. Types of Participants and Interventions Participants included healthcare providers, community health workers, administrative staff, and families involved in birth and death notifications. Interventions involved transmitting information about births or deaths via mobile devices to centralized systems or focal individuals. 12. Data Collection and Analysis Two authors independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence, and a Summary of Findings was prepared. For qualitative data, the SURE framework and GRADE-CERQual approach were applied. 13. Main Results One study from Laos assessed mobile-based birth notifications but showed very low certainty of evidence regarding coverage and timeliness. No studies were identified for mobile-based death notifications. Nineteen studies explored factors influencing implementation, primarily in lowand middle-income settings, focusing on rural and marginalized populations. 14. Factors Influencing Implementation Government commitment, legal frameworks, and health system infrastructure (low confidence). Geographic barriers and network connectivity challenges (moderate confidence). Costs, system maintenance, and data security (low confidence). Human resource availability and healthcare provider training (moderate confidence). Socio-cultural norms and family-related costs (low confidence). Potential inequities in implementation (moderate confidence). 15. Authors’ Conclusions There is a need for more well-designed studies to evaluate the effects of mobile-based birth and death notifications and the factors influencing their implementation. The provision of mobile phones or credits to healthcare providers and community health workers is essential to facilitate these notifications. 16. GRADE Evidence Assessment High certainty: Strong confidence in the true effect being close to the estimated effect. Moderate certainty: Moderate confidence in the effect estimate, with some uncertainty. Low or very low certainty: Limited confidence due to methodological limitations or insufficient evidence.
